<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, gtsummary is structured as an R package designed to create publication‐ready summary and regression tables from data sets. Its primary purpose is to simplify and streamline the creation of highly customizable summary tables (and inline text outputs) that are easy to integrate in reports (e.g., in R Markdown documents) and publications. It leverages well-known tidyverse-compatible packages such as broom, gt, and labelled, and follows a modular design to encapsulate different functionalities (e.g., table summarization, regression result formatting, styling, and output conversion).

Below is a step-by-step guide on how to design the best, most accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Project Type and Scope:
   • This is a full-fledged R package. Its core value is providing a high-level API for summarizing data frames and regression models.
   • Its modules cover data processing, table creation, styling modifications, and exporting or rendering of tables using different output engines (e.g., {gt}, kable, or as a tibble).

2. Break Down the File Structure into Major Components:
   • Source Code (R/ folder): Contains the bulk of the implementation. Nearly every R function is split by its role—from adding statistical info (e.g., add_p, add_ci, add_difference) to formatting (modify_caption, style_pvalue) and output conversion (as_gt, as_kable, as_tibble).
   • Documentation & Man Pages (man/ folder and README/vignettes): Provide detailed user guidance, function documentation, and examples.
   • Testing (tests/ folder): Contains unit tests that validate each function and overall integrity. This folder shows that the package emphasizes reliability.
   • Continuous Integration/Workflow (/.github/workflows): Automated checks (e.g., R-CMD-check, pkgdown builds, code coverage) to ensure consistent quality integration.
   • Package Metadata and Configuration: Files like DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, LICENSE, and pkgdown configuration files define package metadata, export functions, licensing, and documentation site building.
   • Additional Resources: Data examples (data-raw/) and project vignettes (vignettes/) for extended examples and interactive demonstrations.

3. Define the Main Components in Your Diagram:
   – API / User Interface Layer:
     • Represents the functions as exposed to users (e.g., tbl_summary, tbl_regression, tbl_merge).
     • Illustrate how these functions provide entry points to the package.
   – Core Processing Modules:
     • Group the implementation of core functions split by functionality such as:
       ◦ Data Summarization: Function files handling tbl_summary construction.
       ◦ Regression Handling: Modules for tbl_regression and related statistical outputs.
       ◦ Table Manipulation & Formatting: Files for modifying, styling, merging, and stacking tables.
       ◦ Helper Functions: Utility files (e.g., inline_text, select_helpers) that support the core functions.
   – Output Conversion / Rendering Layer:
     • Depict how the processed table objects can be converted to various formats (e.g., as_gt, as_kable, as_hux_table, as_tibble).
   – External Dependencies:
     • Show interactions with external packages such as broom (for tidying up model outputs), gt (for table styling/rendering), and labelled.
   – Testing and Validation:
     • Encompass the tests which ensure each module’s functioning. This reassures the integrity of data transformation and output.
   – Continuous Integration & Documentation:
     • Indicate that CI workflows (GitHub Actions) and documentation tools (like pkgdown) are part of the system, ensuring that updates and changes pass necessary checks before deployment.

4. Illustrate Relationships and Data Flow:
   – Draw directional arrows starting from user calls (via API functions) that pass data into the core processing modules.
   – Show how data flows from raw inputs through transformation functions, then into formatting/conversion layers before output.
   – Include arrows that indicate dependency calls to external libraries and flows from source code to test suites.
   – Represent configuration and documentation generation as side processes that consume the source code information to generate man pages and website documentation.

5. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines for This Project:
   • Use distinct color coding or shapes—for example, rounded rectangles for API components, standard rectangles for core logic modules, and parallelograms for external dependencies.
   • Label each component clearly (e.g., “Data Summarization Module” for tbl_summary-related R files).
   • Include icons or small notes where needed to indicate CI/CD (GitHub workflows) and documentation (vignettes, pkgdown, man pages).
   • Highlight key relationships: For instance, show that the “Table Rendering” modules depend directly on the “Core Processing” modules and then hand off results to output converters.
   • Make sure to capture how user-provided data is transformed by the package by drawing sequential modules and using directional arrows that show how functions like add_p, add_ci, and modify_caption modify table objects step-by-step.

6. Final Diagram Elements:
   – Ensure the diagram includes:
     ◦ Clear labels and legends for components.
     ◦ Directional arrows to show data transformations and inter-module dependencies.
     ◦ Differentiation between core code, documentation, testing, and integration processes.
     ◦ Reference external dependencies and architectural choices (e.g., reliance on tidy approach or modular function design).

By following these detailed guidelines, the resulting system design diagram will clearly and accurately depict the architecture of the gtsummary project, ensuring that every layer—from the exposed API and core functions to the CI/CD pipelines and documentation—is represented. This approach highlights how the package integrates various R functions and modules to deliver its functionality along with robust testing and documentation systems, all of which are critical for a production-level R package. 

Happy diagramming! 
</explanation>
